place.en: The hidden realm · The stone chamber

setup.zh: 墙后面是一间石室，正中一张石台，台上一只玉匣。匣子里，只有一撮土。银月的眼睛，亮得吓人：「息壤。」
setup.en: Behind the wall is a stone chamber: a stone altar in the middle, a jade box on it. In the box, only a pinch of earth. Yinyue's eyes blaze: "Breathing soil."

recap.zh: 石室里的玉匣中，是一撮息壤。你吞了它；它在你身子里长，把五扇又小又乱的门，一扇一扇撑开——五行俱全。练气五层。
recap.en: The jade box in the chamber held a pinch of breathing soil. You swallowed it; it grew inside you and opened your five small, crooked doors one by one — all five elements. Qi Condensation, layer five.

en: A stone altar, a jade box.
In the box, only a pinch of earth.

story.zh:
墙后面，是一间石室。

石室不大，方方正正，四壁都是青石，打磨得光溜溜的，照得出人影。没有灵草，没有法器，也没有前人的骸骨，干干净净，像是昨天才有人扫过。正中一张石台，台上一只玉匣。

可小满一进门，最先看见的，却不是那只玉匣。

石室的地上，离石台三步远的地方，有四个坑。

四个方方的坑，一边一个，排成一个四方，每个坑有碗口那么大，一尺来深，坑底磨得溜光，坑沿磨得发亮。那不是凿出来的，小满一眼便看得出来。他爹教过他看蹄印：鹿蹄印子是鹿踩的，野猪蹄印子是野猪踩的，印子深，是那东西沉；印子磨得发亮，是那东西在这里站了很久很久。这四个坑，是什么东西站出来的。一样极沉极沉的东西，四条腿，在这里站了不知多少年，把石头都站出了坑。然后，它走了。

小满蹲下来，伸手摸了摸那坑底，是凉的。他张开手掌，拇指抵着一个坑的外沿，一拃一拃地量到另一个坑的外沿——猎户量蹄印，向来是这么量的。一拃，两拃，三拃……七拃。他又量了另外三边，边边都是七拃。他量完了，蹲在那里，心里「咯噔」一下。

七拃。

他进山门那天，在正殿里排队等着测灵根，排了足足一个时辰，闲得发慌，眼睛便落在那口空石座上。石座中间那块颜色比别处深的四方印子，他隔着人堆，拿眼睛一拃一拃地量过——那是猎户家孩子的毛病，看见一个印子，不量一量，心里便不踏实。一边七拃。

他站在那四个空坑中间，只觉得后背一阵发凉。正殿里那口石座，空了三百年；这里的四个坑，也空着。一千个人下泗水，捞一口鼎，没捞着——那是他进山门那天，正殿里那个唱名的执事打着呵欠讲的故事。祖师给它留了一口石座，留了三百年，它一天也没有在那石座上站过。它在这里站过。

它站了多少年，他不知道；它去了哪里，他也不知道。他只知道这间石室里的灵气厚得像一口封了几百年的井，外头那条河、那座山、那间讲堂里的灵气，却薄得像一碗刷锅水。褚先生讲了三十年「灵气充盈」，越讲越轻。小满站在四个空坑中间，头一回隐隐约约地觉得，这两件事，也许是一件事。

可他那时候到底只有十三岁，想到这里，便想不下去了。他把这七拃记在了心里，没有写进本子。有些账，写下来反倒记不住。

石室的四壁，远看光溜溜的，走近了，才看得出上头有刻痕。刻得极浅，极细，给几千年的潮气一泡，只剩下一道一道的影子，要侧着脸，借着石壁上那一点微光斜着看，才看得出是画。

东边那面墙上，是水。一层一层的水，浪头卷着浪头，卷得比山还高，水里漂着房子，漂着牛羊，漂着伸着手的人。

南边那面墙上，是一个人，背上背着一只筐，一只手从筐里抓出什么东西，往水里撒。他撒过的地方，水底下冒出一块一块的地来，地上长出草，长出树。那人的脸刻得很模糊，只看得出是低着头的，腰是弯的，像是背着一样极重极重的东西。

西边那面墙上，是九样东西，排成三排，一排三个。每一样都是四四方方，底下四只脚，两只耳朵。小满数了三遍，九个，一个不多，一个不少。

北边那面墙，是空的。整面墙刻满了浅浅的格子，格子里什么都没有，倒像是刻的人刻到这里，还没来得及刻完，便走了。

北边那面墙的最底下，贴着地的地方，有一个很小很小的刻痕。

小满蹲下去看，看了一眼，便愣住了。

那是一只狐狸。蜷着身子，尾巴绕着身子，小小的，刻得比别的都深，都新。他从怀里掏出那块木牌来，凑在旁边一比，一模一样。跟黑松岭那块断碑背面刻着的，也是一模一样。

他抬起头来，看他肩膀上的银月。

银月也在看那只狐狸。她看得很久，一动也不动，一双金色的眼睛里，有什么东西晃了一晃，像是井底的水，给人投进了一颗很小的石子。

小满小声道：「……是你刻的？」

银月道：「……不知道。」

她跳下他的肩膀，走到那只刻出来的狐狸跟前，低下头，拿鼻子碰了碰它。碰完了，她在那里站了一会儿，尾巴垂着。然后她转过身来，又跳回了他肩膀上，一句话也没有说。

小满也没有再问。他想，一个连自己名字都要想半天的妖王，在一面几千年的墙上看见一只跟自己一模一样的狐狸，心里大概也不怎么好受。有些账，债主自己都没想起来，旁人便不好去催。

他走到石台前，打开了玉匣。

匣子里，只有**一撮土**。

黄褐色的，松松的，一小撮，刚好铺满匣底，普普通通，跟他家后院那块种不出东西的地里的土没什么两样——不，比那还不如。他家后院的土，好歹闻起来有一股锈味儿；这一撮，什么味儿也没有。

小满盯着那撮土看了半天，道：「……就这？」

他肩膀上的银月，却没有说话。

他转过头去看它。只见它一双金色的眼睛亮得吓人，亮得像两盏灯，盯着那撮土，一眨不眨，尾巴尖上的毛，一根一根，全竖了起来。

它一字一字地道：「息壤。」

小满道：「什么？」

银月的声音都在抖：「会自己长的土。」

小满道：「土还会自己长？」

银月道：「会。你给它一粒，它长出一撮；给它一撮，它长出一座山。当年——」它说到这里停住了，眉头皱起来，像是在很深很深的井里捞一样东西，捞了半天，只捞上来半桶，「——当年天上发大水。不是凡间的水，是天上漫下来的水，一直漫到人间，淹了九州。有个人，叫鲧，从天帝那里，把这土偷了出来……」

小满道：「偷？」

银月道：「偷。天帝不给，他就偷。偷出来，往洪水里一撒，水涨一尺，土长一丈，水涨一丈，土长一里——拿会长的土，去堵会涨的水。」

小满道：「那不是挺好？」

银月道：「好什么。天帝知道了，叫火神把他杀了，杀在羽山的郊外。」她顿了一顿，声音低下去，「……杀了三年，身子不烂。后来有人拿刀剖开他的肚子，肚子里……」

小满道：「肚子里是什么？」

银月道：「是一个人。他儿子。」

小满打了个寒战：「……肚子里长出儿子来？」

银月道：「本王讲古，凡人插什么嘴。」

小满便闭了嘴。她却也停了一停，像是那一句打断，把什么东西惊走了。她把脸扭开，接着往下说，说得又快又硬：「那儿子叫禹。天帝后来想明白了，不杀他，给他土，叫他接着治水。禹不堵，他挖，他疏，他把那土一把一把铺在九州的地上，铺平了，定下了九州。后来他铸了九口鼎，一州一口……」

她说到这里，忽然停住了。

她盯着石室地上那四个空坑，盯了很久很久，久到石室里那一丝暖风吹过去，又吹回来。她没有再往下说。

小满后来许多年以后，在一本书上读到了这个故事。那书叫《山海经》，写得比银月说的短得多，只有几行，鲧偷土，鲧被杀，鲧腹里生禹，禹铺土定九州，一句多余的话也没有。杀了三年身子不烂那一截，书里没有；肚子剖开那一截，书里也没有。他那时候才明白，银月那天说的，有一半是书上的，有一半是她自己的——不是她记错了，是她记得的，比书上多。

那天在石室里，他只问了一句：「……它能干什么？」

银月转过头来，盯着他，道：「吞下去。」

小满吓了一跳：「吞——吞土？」

银月道：「吞下去！」

小满道：「我娘说，吃土是要闹肚子的——」

银月道：「你娘说得对！可这不是土！」

小满道：「你刚才说它是土。」

银月尾巴上的毛「蓬」的一声，全炸了开来，炸成一个毛球：「——你到底吞不吞！」
story.en:
Behind the wall was a stone chamber.

Not large, perfectly square, the four walls of bluestone polished so smooth they gave back a reflection. No herbs, no magic tools, no bones of those before — clean, as if someone had swept it yesterday. In the middle a stone altar, and on the altar a jade box.

But when Xiaoman came in, the first thing he saw was not the jade box.

On the floor, three paces from the altar, were four pits.

Four square pits, one to each side, set out in a square, each the size of a bowl's mouth and a foot deep, their bottoms worn slick and their rims worn shining. They had not been chiselled — Xiaoman saw that at a glance. His father had taught him to read hoofprints: a deer's print is made by a deer, a boar's by a boar; a deep print means a heavy beast, a print worn shiny means the beast stood there a very long time. These four pits had been stood into being. Something very, very heavy, with four legs, had stood here who knew how many years, till it stood the stone into pits. And then it had gone.

Xiaoman crouched and felt the bottom of a pit: cold. He spread his hand, set his thumb against the outer edge of one pit, and measured span by span to the outer edge of the next — that is how hunters measure a print. One span, two, three… seven. He measured the other three sides: seven every side. When he was done he stayed crouched there, and his heart gave a lurch.

Seven spans.

The day he entered the sect he had queued a whole hour in the main hall waiting for the root test, bored to death, and his eyes had come to rest on the empty stone seat. In the middle of that seat was a square mark darker than the rest, and across the crowd he had measured it with his eyes, span by span — a hunter's child's habit: see a mark and not measure it, and you're uneasy. Seven spans to a side.

Standing among the four empty pits, he felt a chill down his back. The stone seat in the main hall had stood empty three hundred years; the four pits here were empty too. A thousand men went down into the Si to dredge up a cauldron and got nothing — the story the steward calling names had told, yawning, the day he entered the sect. The founder had kept a stone seat for it, kept it three hundred years, and it had never stood on that seat a single day. It had stood here.

How many years it stood here, he didn't know; where it went, he didn't know either. He only knew that the qi in this chamber was thick as a well sealed a few hundred years, while the qi in the river outside, the mountain, the lecture hall, was thin as dishwater. Master Chu had said "spirit qi abounds" for thirty years, softer and softer. Standing among the four empty pits, Xiaoman felt for the first time, dimly, that these two things might be one thing.

But he was only thirteen, and there his thinking stopped. He kept the seven spans in his heart and did not write them in his notebook. Some accounts, written down, are harder to remember.

The chamber's walls, smooth from a distance, showed marks up close — carved very shallow, very fine, and after thousands of years of damp only shadows of lines were left; you had to turn your face sideways and look slantwise by the faint light off the stone to see they were pictures.

On the east wall, water. Layer on layer of it, wave rolling over wave, rolling higher than mountains; houses floating in it, oxen and sheep, people with hands outstretched.

On the south wall, a man with a basket on his back, one hand taking something from the basket and scattering it on the water. Where he scattered, land rose from under the water piece by piece, and on the land grass grew, and trees. The man's face was carved blurred; you could see only that his head was bowed and his back bent, as if under something very, very heavy.

On the west wall, nine things, in three rows of three. Each was square, with four legs beneath and two ears. Xiaoman counted three times: nine, not one more, not one fewer.

The north wall was empty. The whole wall was carved with faint squares, nothing in them, as if whoever carved it had got this far and left before he could finish.

At the very bottom of the north wall, against the floor, was a very, very small carving.

Xiaoman crouched to look, looked once, and froze.

It was a fox. Curled up, tail wrapped round its body, small, cut deeper and fresher than the rest. He took the token from his coat and held it beside it: the same. And the same, too, as the one carved on the back of the broken stele at Black Pine Ridge.

He looked up at Yinyue on his shoulder.

Yinyue was looking at the fox too. She looked a long time without moving, and in her golden eyes something wavered, like water at the bottom of a well when someone drops in a very small pebble.

Xiaoman whispered, "…Did you carve it?"

"…Don't know," said Yinyue.

She jumped down from his shoulder, went to the carved fox, bent her head, and touched it with her nose. Then she stood there a while, tail hanging. Then she turned and jumped back onto his shoulder without a word.

Xiaoman didn't ask again. He thought: a demon queen who has to think half a day for her own name, seeing on a wall thousands of years old a fox exactly like herself — she can't feel very good. Some debts, when the creditor herself hasn't remembered them, it isn't for others to press.

He went to the altar and opened the jade box.

In the box was only **a pinch of earth**.

Yellow-brown, loose, a little pinch, just enough to cover the bottom — utterly ordinary, no different from the dirt in his family's back plot where nothing would grow. No — worse. His back plot at least smelled of rust; this pinch smelled of nothing at all.

Xiaoman stared at it a good while. "…That's it?"

Yinyue on his shoulder said nothing.

He turned to look at her. Her golden eyes were frighteningly bright, bright as two lamps, fixed on the pinch of earth without a blink, the fur at the tip of her tail standing up hair by hair.

Word by word she said: "Xirang."

"What?"

Her voice was shaking. "Earth that grows by itself."

"Earth grows by itself?"

"It does. Give it a grain, it grows a pinch; give it a pinch, it grows a mountain. Back then —" she stopped and frowned, as if fishing for something in a very, very deep well, and after all that brought up only half a bucket — "— back then there was a great flood from heaven. Not mortal water: water that spilled down from the sky, all the way to the human world, and drowned the Nine Provinces. There was a man called Gun, who took this earth from the Lord of Heaven by stealth…"

"Stole it?"

"Stole it. The Lord of Heaven wouldn't give it, so he stole it. Stole it and scattered it on the flood: the water rose a foot, the earth grew ten; the water rose ten, the earth grew a li — earth that grows, to dam water that rises."

"Isn't that good?"

"Good how. The Lord of Heaven found out and had the fire god kill him — killed him in the wilds of Mount Yu." She paused, and her voice dropped. "…Killed three years, and the body didn't rot. Later someone cut open his belly with a knife, and in the belly…"

"What was in the belly?"

"A man. His son."

Xiaoman shivered. "…A son grew in his belly?"

"When I tell the old stories, a mortal doesn't butt in."

So Xiaoman shut his mouth. But she paused too, as if the interruption had startled something away. She turned her face aside and went on, fast and hard: "The son was called Yu. The Lord of Heaven thought better of it later, didn't kill him, gave him the earth, and told him to finish taming the water. Yu didn't dam — he dug, he drained, he spread that earth handful by handful over the lands of the Nine Provinces, spread it flat, and fixed the Nine Provinces. Later he cast nine cauldrons, one for each province…"

Here she stopped short.

She stared at the four empty pits on the floor a long, long time — long enough for that thread of warm wind to blow across the chamber and back. She said no more.

Many years later Xiaoman read this story in a book. The book was the *Classic of Mountains and Seas*, and it told it much more briefly than Yinyue — only a few lines: Gun steals the earth, Gun is killed, Yu is born from Gun's belly, Yu spreads the earth and fixes the Nine Provinces, not one word to spare. The three years without rotting weren't in the book; the belly cut open wasn't in the book either. Only then did he understand that half of what Yinyue told that day came from the book and half was her own — not misremembered: she remembered more than the book did.

That day in the chamber he asked only: "…What does it do?"

Yinyue turned and fixed him with her eyes. "Swallow it."

Xiaoman jumped. "Sw— swallow earth?"

"Swallow it!"

"My ma says eating dirt gives you the runs —"

"Your ma is right! But this isn't dirt!"

"You just said it was earth."

The fur on Yinyue's tail went *poof* — all of it, into a ball. "— Are you going to swallow it or not!"

exits._doors: The page's moment after this exit (story.mjs node `doors`): the five doors open one by one, a seal and a line each, in ink — colour is for 银月's memories alone.

doors.zh: 第一扇，金。「铮」的一声——是爷爷那张弓的弦。
doors.en: The first, Metal. A twang — the string of Grandpa's bow.

doors.zh: 第二扇，木。吱吱呀呀，像黑松岭的松树，在没有风的夜里自己挪了一步。
doors.en: The second, Wood. Creak by creak, like the pines of Black Pine Ridge moving a step on a windless night.

doors.zh: 第三扇，水。一冷——是那一盆洗髓的水；冷过了，化成一条清河。
doors.en: The third, Water. A chill — the marrow-washing basin; then it melts into a clear river.

doors.zh: 第四扇，火。灶膛里的火。娘拨一拨柴：「打不过就跑，跑不丢人。」
doors.en: The fourth, Fire. The fire in the stove. Ma pokes the wood: "If you can't win, run. No shame in running."

doors.zh: 第五扇，土。一股锈味儿，越开越淡——底下，是开春翻开的新土。
doors.en: The fifth, Earth. A smell of rust, fainter as it opens — and underneath, new earth turned in spring.

story.zh:
小满看看那撮土，又看看她。他想起山谷里那天早上，她捧着那个饼角放进他手心，郑重得像捧着一方传国玉玺；想起柴垛上那一夜，她说「本王答不动了」；想起柴房后头那一夜，她淡成一缕烟，最后剩下半句「下次，打回去」。他想，这个妖王，这个嘴比天大、肚子比谁都饿、连自己名字都要想半天的妖王，这辈子，还没有害过他。

他把那撮土倒在手心里，一口吞了下去。

那撮土一进嘴，便化了。

化得像一口温水，顺着喉咙往下滑，滑进肚子，滑进丹田，停住了。停了一会儿，然后，它开始**长**。

他觉得出它来。它在他丹田里像一粒种子，「啪」地一声，破开了壳，伸出一根根须子，须子又细又软，却有一股说不出的劲道，往他身子的每一个角落里扎去。扎进经脉，扎进骨头，扎进皮肉底下，最后，扎进了那五扇门。

那五扇门，是他的灵根。金、木、水、火、土，五扇门，又小又乱，歪歪扭扭，像一只漏勺上随手戳出来的五个洞。测灵石亮起来的那天，满殿的人笑，笑的便是这五扇门。

那些须子扎进门缝里，便开始往外撑。

头一扇给撑开的，是金。

那扇门「铮」的一声，开了一线，那一声，他听着耳熟——是爷爷那张弓的弦。他在溪边头一回拉开那张弓，手指一松，弦就是这么「铮」的一声，震得他虎口发麻。那扇门一线一线地开，每开一线，便「铮」一声，一声比一声亮，亮得他牙根发酸。

第二扇是木。那扇门开得最慢，吱吱呀呀，像黑松岭里那些黑皮的松树，在没有风的夜里，自己往旁边挪了一步。他闻见了松脂的味道，闻见了树干上刀口里一丝一丝往外渗的那股清苦——他刻了四十一道记号，第一道刻歪了。

第三扇是水。那扇门一开，他便冷得打了个寒战，冷得像那一夜泡在娘洗衣裳的大木盆里，墨绿的水，咕嘟咕嘟冒着泡，一千只蚂蚁在骨头缝里开会。可那冷只冷了一下，跟着便化开了，化成一条河，河水是清的，一直流，一直流，流到很远很远的地方去。

第四扇是火。那扇门后头是暖的，暖得他鼻子一酸——是灶膛里的火。他娘蹲在灶前烙饼，火光一闪一闪地照在她脸上，她拿火钳拨一拨柴，道：「打不过就跑，跑不丢人。」

第五扇是土。那扇门最沉，撑了很久很久，才撑开一条缝。缝里透出来的，是一股味道，他一闻便知道是什么：是他家后院那块地，那块种什么都不长、一股锈味儿的地。可那扇门越开越大，那股锈味儿便越来越淡，淡到后来，底下透出另一股味道来，香的，暖的，像是开春头一场雨下透了，一锄头翻开的新土。吴婆婆说过：那时候，这地，是香的。

五扇门，一扇一扇，撑开，撑大，撑直。原先又小又乱，如今一扇比一扇宽，一扇比一扇正，一扇比一扇亮。

他跪在石台前头，浑身发抖，却不是疼。那感觉比疼还难熬，是涨，涨得他整个人像一只给灌满了水的皮囊，又像一片刚下过一场透雨的地，每一寸都有东西在往外冒，冒得他想喊，又喊不出来，只把牙关咬得咯咯地响。

他不知道自己跪了多久。

等他睁开眼睛的时候，石室里静悄悄的。他扶着石台站起身来，腿是软的，一步一晃，走到那面磨得光溜溜的石壁跟前。石壁里照出一个人影，蓬着头，一脸的汗，灰袍子给汗湿透了，贴在身上。那是他自己。可那人影的皮肤底下，有光。

五种颜色的光，在他皮肤底下流。金的，青的，黑的，红的，黄的，一种不少，一道一道，像五条小河，从他的心口流出去，流到手指尖，又从手指尖流回来，流过一圈，又是一圈。每一种都亮得刺眼，比测灵石上亮过的任何一种都亮。

银月蹲在石台上，看着那五道光，看了很久，才开口，声音很轻：「……五行俱全。五门俱开。」

小满问：「这很难得么？」

银月道：「五门俱开，五行便能相生。木生火，火生土，土生金，金生水，水生木，转成一个圈，首尾相接，不断，不漏。」她顿了一顿，「天底下的功法，要金的有金，要木的有木，要五行一齐转的——你也有。天底下，没有一门功法，你修不了。」

她又顿了一顿，这一回顿得很久，久到小满以为她又要睡着了。然后，她的声音轻得像一片落下来的叶子：「从今天起，你不是漏勺了。」

小满低头看着自己的手，看着那五道光从手指缝里流过去。他道：「……那我是什么？」

银月想了想，道：「……水缸。」

小满没有接话。

她又补了一句：「很大的水缸。」

小满笑了。

他咧着嘴笑，笑得很傻，笑着笑着，眼泪便流了下来。他想起褚先生那撮翘起来的山羊胡子，想起满堂的哄笑，想起测灵石上那块用五种碎布拼成的抹布，想起执事拖长了调子念的那四个字：下下之资。他想起舅舅那一百六十级，想起孙二狗那一拳，想起柴房后头那二十三下。他想起他娘，在灶间的油灯底下，拿过他的手，放在竹简上第一个字上，道：「这个字，念『吹』。吹气的吹。」

他没有擦眼泪。他吸了一口气。

第五层的关口开了以后，石室里的灵气却还厚着。

他试着又吸了一口，那灵气照旧哗哗地涌过来，涌得他丹田里满满当当，满得往外溢。他心里算了一笔账：照这么吸下去，再吸半天，第六层的门槛，也许便摸得着了。外门的规矩，练气六层，大比上已是能跟老弟子过招的；马小宝家里一车一车地往山上送丹药，送到今天，也不过一层。半天，六层。这笔账，怎么算都划算。

他便又吸了一口。

这一口吸下去，他觉出不对来了。丹田里那五扇门还开着，可门后头那一圈五色的光，转得慢了，转得沉了，像一口锅里的粥，熬得太稠，勺子搅不动。他再吸，那灵气便在经脉里堵着，胀着，胀得他胸口发闷，太阳穴一跳一跳地疼。

胸口的木牌凉凉地贴着他，一个很困的声音在他耳朵里说了两个字：「够了。」

小满道：「还没够。再吸半天，就六层了。」

那声音道：「……你娘给你起的名字，叫什么？」

小满愣了一愣。

他想起了过年那天夜里，他娘坐在灶前，拿火钳拨着灶膛里的灰，给他讲他这个名字：满了就要溢出来，溢出来就糟践了；饱了一点，还没满，还知道饿。知道饿，才知道别人也饿。他又想起离家前一夜，吴婆婆坐在门槛上摇着那把破蒲扇，说的那一句：饿了，就吃；饱了，就放下。

他坐在那里，丹田里那一锅稠粥还在胀着。他慢慢地把那口还没吸完的气，吐了出去。

吐出去的那一刻，胸口一松。那一圈五色的光，又转起来了，转得轻快，转得匀，一圈，又一圈。

他睁开眼睛，石室里的灵气还厚厚地积着，像一口井，他只舀走了浅浅的一层。他看着那口井，心里没来由地想：这口井，攒了几百年，才攒下这么一点。他舀走了三天，舀得够了。剩下的，留给它自己。

他后来想起这件事，常常觉得好笑：一个五行杂灵根、下下之资的漏勺，头一回变成了水缸，头一件学会的事，竟不是怎么把缸装满，是怎么不装满。
story.en:
Xiaoman looked at the pinch of earth, then at her. He thought of that morning in the valley, when she held the corner of flatbread in both hands and laid it in his palm, solemn as if handing over the imperial seal; of the night on the woodpile, when she said "I can't answer any more"; of the night behind the woodshed, when she faded to a wisp of smoke and all that was left was half a sentence: "Next time, hit back." He thought: this demon queen — mouth bigger than the sky, hungrier than anyone, who has to think half a day for her own name — has never once done him harm.

He tipped the earth into his palm and swallowed it in one gulp.

The earth melted the moment it entered his mouth.

Melted like a mouthful of warm water, slid down his throat, into his belly, into his dantian, and stopped. It stayed still a while, and then it began to **grow**.

He could feel it. It sat in his dantian like a seed, and — *pop* — split its shell and put out roots, fine and soft, yet with a strength he couldn't name, driving into every corner of his body. Into his channels, into his bones, under his flesh — and last of all, into the five doors.

The five doors were his roots. Metal, Wood, Water, Fire, Earth: five doors, small and disordered, crooked, like five holes poked at random in a skimmer. The day the testing stone lit up, the whole hall laughed, and it was these five doors they laughed at.

The roots worked into the cracks of the doors and began to push them open.

The first door pushed open was Metal.

It opened a crack with a *twang* — and the sound was familiar: the string of his grandfather's bow. The first time he drew that bow, by the stream, he let go and the string went *twang* just so, numbing the web of his thumb. The door opened a crack at a time, and each crack went *twang*, each brighter than the last, till his teeth ached.

The second was Wood. It opened slowest, creak by creak, like the black-barked pines of Black Pine Ridge on a windless night moving a step aside by themselves. He smelled pine resin, and the clean bitterness seeping thread by thread from knife cuts in the trunks — he had carved forty-one marks, and the first was crooked.

The third was Water. The moment it opened he shivered with cold, cold like that night soaking in his mother's big washtub — the dark-green water bubbling, a thousand ants holding council in the cracks of his bones. But the cold lasted only a moment, then melted and became a river, a clear river, flowing on and on to somewhere very far away.

The fourth was Fire. Behind that door it was warm — so warm his nose stung. The fire in the stove. His mother crouching before the stove baking flatbread, firelight flickering on her face; she poked the wood with the tongs and said: "If you can't win, run. There's no shame in running."

The fifth was Earth. It was heaviest; it took a long, long time to push open even a crack. What came through the crack was a smell, and he knew it at once: his family's back plot, the plot where nothing grew, that smelled of rust. But the wider the door opened the fainter the rust grew, till underneath came another smell — fragrant, warm, like new earth turned by the hoe after the first soaking rain of spring. Granny Wu had said: back then, this land was fragrant.

Five doors, one by one, pushed open, pushed wide, pushed straight. Once small and disordered, now each wider than the last, each truer, each brighter.

He knelt before the altar shaking all over, and not with pain. It was worse than pain — a swelling, as if he were a waterskin filled to bursting, or a field after a soaking rain, every inch of it pushing something up; he wanted to shout and couldn't, only clenched his teeth till they chattered.

He didn't know how long he knelt.

When he opened his eyes the chamber was silent. He pulled himself up by the altar, legs weak, wobbling at every step, to the polished wall. In the stone was the reflection of a boy — hair wild, face running with sweat, grey robe soaked and clinging. It was himself. But under the skin of that reflection there was light.

Five colours of light, flowing under his skin. Gold, green, black, red, yellow — not one missing, streak after streak, like five little rivers flowing out from his heart to his fingertips and back from his fingertips, one circuit, then another. Each dazzling, brighter than any colour the testing stone had ever shown.

Yinyue crouched on the altar watching those five lights a long time before she spoke, very softly: "…All five elements. All five doors open."

"Is that rare?" Xiaoman asked.

"Five doors open, and the five elements can feed one another. Wood feeds Fire, Fire feeds Earth, Earth feeds Metal, Metal feeds Water, Water feeds Wood — round in a circle, head to tail, unbroken, not leaking." She paused. "Every art under heaven — want Metal, you have Metal; want Wood, you have Wood; want all five turning together — you have that too. There's not an art under heaven you can't cultivate."

She paused again, so long this time that Xiaoman thought she'd fallen asleep. Then her voice came light as a falling leaf: "From today, you're not a skimmer."

Xiaoman looked down at his hands, at the five lights running between his fingers. "…Then what am I?"

Yinyue thought. "…A water vat."

Xiaoman said nothing.

She added: "A very big water vat."

Xiaoman laughed.

He grinned, laughing like a fool, and as he laughed the tears ran. He thought of Master Chu's jutting goat's beard, of the whole hall roaring, of the testing stone like a dishrag patched from five colours of scraps, of the steward drawling out those words: bottom of the bottom. He thought of his uncle's hundred and sixty steps, of Sun Ergou's punch, of the twenty-three blows behind the woodshed. He thought of his mother under the oil lamp in the kitchen, taking his hand and laying it on the first character of the bamboo scroll: "This one is read *chui*. *Chui*, to blow."

He didn't wipe away the tears. He drew a breath.

After the gate of the fifth level opened, the qi in the chamber was still thick.

He tried another breath, and the qi came rushing in as before, filling his dantian full, so full it spilled. He did a sum in his head: breathe on like this another half day and he might touch the threshold of the sixth level. By the rules of the outer court, at the sixth level of Qi Refining you could cross hands with old disciples at the contest; the Ma family had been sending pills up the mountain by the cartload, and after all that Xiaobao had gone up — one level. Half a day, the sixth. However you worked that sum, it paid.

So he took another breath.

With that breath he felt something wrong. The five doors in his dantian were still open, but the five-coloured circle behind them turned slower, heavier, like porridge boiled too thick in a pot, too stiff for the ladle. He breathed again, and the qi jammed in his channels, swelling, till his chest felt tight and his temples throbbed.

The token lay cool against his chest, and a very sleepy voice said two words in his ear: "Enough."

"Not yet," said Xiaoman. "Half a day more and it's the sixth."

The voice said: "…The name your mother gave you — what is it?"

Xiaoman was taken aback.

He thought of that New Year's night, his mother by the stove poking the ashes with the tongs, telling him about his name: full to the brim, it spills, and spilled is wasted; a little full, not yet brimming, still knows hunger. Knowing hunger, you know others are hungry too. And he thought of the night before he left home, Granny Wu on her threshold waving that ragged palm fan, saying: hungry, eat; full, put it down.

He sat there, the stiff porridge in his dantian still swelling. Slowly he let out the breath he hadn't finished drawing.

The moment it went out, his chest loosened. The five-coloured circle turned again, lightly, evenly, round and round.

He opened his eyes. The qi still lay thick in the chamber like a well; he had ladled off only a shallow layer. Looking at that well, he thought for no reason: this well took a few hundred years to save up this much. He had ladled three days; he had ladled enough. The rest he'd leave to it.

Later, remembering it, he often found it funny: a mixed five-element root, bottom of the bottom, a skimmer, turned into a water vat for the first time — and the first thing he learned was not how to fill the vat, but how not to.
